extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, adjutant general staff, government attorneys, and administrators dealing with territorial/military law
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal rules and administrative standards governing the application of territorial law, military-civil relations, uniforms, Philippine/Alaskan administration, and volunteer army mustering and discharge. The page collects official opinions and holdings that guide officers and administrators on jurisdiction, authority, and procedural duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of territorial statutes on military reservations
rubrics_metrics.description: A Territorial statute is operative upon a military reservation within the Territory so long as it does not conflict with the laws of the United States or with the military administration or legitimate operations of the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An Arizona statute penalizing sale of intoxicating liquor to Indians could not legally affect sale of such beer to enlisted soldiers when sale to soldiers was permitted by Army regulations. (Cited opinions: P. 48, 464, Aug. 1891; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation of United States instrumentalities by territorial governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of a Territory or territorial possession of the United States cannot, unaided by legislation, impose a tax upon an instrumentality of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where service by a territorial or insular agency is necessary, it is recommended to place it on a contractual basis with compensation not to exceed statutory rates. (Citation: C. 21469, Apr. 24, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with territorial court subpoenas by military
rubrics_metrics.description: The military should obey the subpoenas of the district courts of Territories, which (under section 1910, R.S.) have the same jurisdiction as U.S. circuit and district courts in cases under the Constitution and laws of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 877 and 911, R.S., prescribe the form and effect of such subpoenas; a subpoena served upon an officer or soldier that conforms substantially to these forms should be complied with. (R. 54, 124, July, 1887; C. 1469, Apr. 24, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alaskan treaty citizenship rule
rubrics_metrics.description: By the treaty of cession with Russia, subjects of that nation inhabiting the Territory of Alaska at the date of the treaty and continuing to remain such inhabitants for three years became American citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treaty neither mentions nor refers to British subjects or subjects of any foreign nation other than Russia; such persons residing in the Territory can become citizens only by the mode prescribed by U.S. naturalization laws. (R. 38, 555, Apr. 12, 1877.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of posse comitatus and marshals' authority in Alaska
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'posse comitatus act' (June 18, 1878) is, by section 29 of the act of June 6, 1900, made inoperative in Alaska; the U.S. marshal is made the judge of the necessity of using military force in Alaska.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commanding officer of military forces in Alaska should assist the marshal in maintaining order; the marshal determines the emergency necessitating military force and the commanding officer directs employment of the troops to accomplish the marshal's purposes. (C. 3119; Feb. 13, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of surplus military coal to civilians in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by reason of emergency and demands of humanity, it is necessary to sell small amounts of coal to civilians in Alaska and military supply is in excess, such sales may be made at net cost, delivered at place of sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sales should be reported to Congress at its next meeting. (C. 19307, Mar. 2 and Oct. 13, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial telegraph credit business in Alaska
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Secretary of War has discretion under the act of May 26, 1900, to allow commercial telegraph business to be done on credit, existing regulations do not authorize credit messages over Alaskan telegraph lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until new regulations are published authorizing credit, telegraph business in Alaska should be conducted on a cash basis. (C. 20409, Sept. 21, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of telegrams by civil authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A request by the U.S. marshal in Alaska to examine telegrams sent over Alaskan telegraph lines by parties suspected of robbery is lawful upon request of the proper court or civil authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such telegrams are not privileged. (C. 20086, July 19, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Military issuance of liquor permits to Alaska ended by civil government act
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the act of May 17, 1884 (establishing a civil government for Alaska), military authorities could no longer legally issue permits for the introduction of liquors into Alaska under General Order 57 of 1874.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 14 of the civil government act is deemed implicitly to repeal, as to Alaska, that portion of section 2139, R.S., empowering the Secretary of War to authorize such introduction. (R. 50, 529, July, 1886.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Road commission authority to construct wooden tramways
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alaskan road commission has authority to construct a wooden tramway over portions of roads and trails where that form of road will best subserve the purposes of traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held within commission authority. (C. 18173, June 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on transferring Army-purchased property to tax-funded list
rubrics_metrics.description: A request to transfer a horse purchased out of Army appropriations to the list of property purchased out of tax funds was held unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a transfer would not be lawful. (C. 18173, Aug. 2, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to obtain temporary licenses for roadway rights-of-way
rubrics_metrics.description: A conveyance consisting of a license from a railroad company for a period of five years, at the expiration of which the roadway is to be restored to the licensor, will be within the authority of the Alaskan road commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held lawful in the operation of commission authority. (C. 18173, Apr. 10, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation of civilian U.S. employees to perform road labor in Alaska
rubrics_metrics.description: When certain civilian employees were required to perform labor on roads in Alaska under the act of April 27, 1904, the War Department is without power to excuse compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The employee should present his claim for exemption to the proper precinct authorities, accompanied by a certificate showing the character of his employment and that his entire services are necessary in the administration of the regiment, post, or depot. (C. 20327.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Philippine Constabulary status and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Philippine Constabulary is a force of peace officers created by an act of the Philippine Commission; duties prescribed by law chiefly relate to maintenance of public order and enforcement of the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resistance to enforcement is encountered or the peace is threatened, it is their duty to overcome opposition and restore civil order using such and so much force as is necessary. (C. 17608, Feb. 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Command relationship between Constabulary and Philippine Scouts
rubrics_metrics.description: The operation of the act of January 30, 1903 has vested in certain officers of the Philippine Constabulary the same power of military command over companies of the Philippine Scouts (ordered to assist the constabulary) as is exercised by Army officers over commands assigned by the President or military superiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chief of the Philippine Constabulary's control is derived from Philippine Commission legislation and orders of the civil governor; his authority over scouts is strictly military and applicable where the disturbance is limited and order can be restored by civil agencies with scout assistance. (C. 17508, Feb. 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Constabulary officers commanding troops aboard transports
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Philippine Constabulary (rank of colonel and assistant chief) prosecuting a voyage to Manila on an Army transport was held not entitled to command the troops on board under the 122nd article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such power to command is restricted, in operation of the act of Jan. 30, 1903, to command of Philippine troops in certain emergency conditions. (C. 17508, Feb. 15, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of honorary or conferred rank in Constabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: The rank of colonel conferred upon an Army officer as assistant chief of the Philippine Constabulary entitles the officer to the same precedence, dignities, and privileges to which a colonel in the line or staff of the Army is entitled by law, regulations, or War Dept orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is also entitled to the same consideration in assignment of stateroom accommodations upon an Army transport as a colonel of the line or staff would receive. (C. 17508, Feb. 15, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President's duty and authority regarding Canal Zone public order
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the State of Panama to maintain public order within its territory; if the laws are set at defiance or their execution hindered and the fact is determined to the President's satisfaction, it becomes his duty to remove such hindrances and take necessary steps to restore civil order within the limits of his treaty jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President can direct the Secretary of War to issue appropriate instructions to the commanding officer of forces in the Canal Zone to take steps calculated to remove obstacles to execution of the treaty and restore public order in Colon, Panama, and adjacent territories. (C. 17164, Nov. 15, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of the dignity of the uniform and exclusion from public places
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of soldiers from a public place of amusement (e.g., a skating rink) in a Territory because they were in uniform was held to be a violation of the act of March 1, 1911, for the protection of the dignity and honor of the uniform of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commanding officer pursued the proper course in instituting a prosecution against a proprietor who attempted such exclusion; convictions have been obtained under relevant statutes. (C. 18958, Dec. 7, 1911; Jan. 23, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of ticket holders and status of theater tickets
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of persons to purchase tickets to a place of amusement or of ticket holders to enter for which they hold tickets depend entirely on State law; a theater ticket is a license revocable by the licensor before it has been tendered at the door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the purchaser of a particular seat has more than a license — his right of entrance is in the nature of a lease and is not affected by the fact he may be a soldier in uniform. (C. 18958, Dec. 11, 1905; Nov. 28, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution for impersonating an officer
rubrics_metrics.description: When it appears that any person, with intent to defraud the United States or any person, falsely assumes or pretends to be an officer or employee (by wearing a uniform or otherwise), the case should be referred to the Department of Justice for prosecution under the act of April 18, 1884 (23 Stat. 11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple referrals and prosecutions have been made under this statute. (C. 14779, various dates 1906–1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and legal status of the Volunteer Army
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'Volunteer Army' comprehensively denotes a temporary military organization which the Government employs and maintains in time of war or public danger, comprising persons who engage directly with the United States, conscripts, and State militia called into U.S. service by the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volunteers raised directly by the United States are usually termed 'volunteers'; the President cannot raise or maintain volunteers at will without express authority of Congress; the legal status of persons claiming to be volunteers depends on whether an act of Congress authorized their raising and employment at the time. (C. 1301, May, 1895; C. 1377, May, 1895; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between volunteers and militia once mustered
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteer officers, once mustered into the service of the United States, and while they remain in that service, do not differ substantially from Regular officers in their status, rights, or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though volunteers' tenure may be briefer, their legal status while serving is substantially like Regular officers. (R. 34-, 449, Sept., 1873; C. 5075, Sept. 28, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster-in rules and record finality
rubrics_metrics.description: Muster-in rolls are the formal official record of enrollment; mustering in is generally irrevocable unless tainted with fraud; remustering is not allowed in cases where a man was never mustered in or the organization never legally existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various historical and statutory nuances control when mustering in is required (e.g., Civil War, Spanish War volunteers), and constructive muster doctrines apply in some contexts. (Synopsis: Musters I–III; examples and cases cited throughout pages 1039–1044.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Muster-out authority and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department order to muster out has the force of law; muster-out is the termination of military service of an organization, an officer, or an enlisted man (even if the organization is not disbanded until later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules on date of muster-out: the true date is the actual date of muster-out regardless of advance dates or discharge certificate entries; dates cannot be changed (no nunc pro tunc); retention in service after muster-out and special classes (deserters, absentees, prisoners of war) have specified rules. Records of organizations are deposited in the War Department. (Synopsis: Muster-out IV; pages 1045–1050.)
